# Experimental Medicine Application Platform
	## Background and problem statement
	University College London Hospital will acquire its own integrated electronic health care record (EHR) in 2019.[^1] However, the history of electronic health care data goes back much further, and a substantial portion of any hospital's operations depends on electronic systems. 
	Secondary use of these data for research raises two major concerns. For the public, the key concern is privacy. This has been highlighted by the controversial *'Care.data'* programme[^2] in 2013, and the publicly censured collaboration between the Royal Free Hospital and Google DeepMind in 2017.[^3] For the health care provider, the key concern is that secondary use does not affect the primary function of clinical and operational systems. 
	Outside health care, the tools required for secondary use of data have concurrently evolved and converged regardless of whether the task is labelled as research, audit, business analytics, or even software and application development. The emerging paradigm is that these are connected and collaborative projects. As a consequence, open source technologies dominate whether these are deep neural networks ([TensorFlow](https://www.tensorflow.org)), the MapReduce programming model for big data ([Hadoop](https://hadoop.apache.org)), data science tools ([R](https://www.r-project.org) and [Python](https://www.scipy.org)), version control ([Git](https://git-scm.com)) and testing and quality assurance ([Jenkins](https://jenkins.io)).
	This convergence presents a problem for health since external connectivity is a risk to both privacy and the security of operational systems. Existing solutions for secondary use simply erect a walled garden around the data. Within which, the provided tooling in inevitably limited, and  collaboration, version control, and testing are crippled. This is true of information services within the hospital, of UCL's data safe haven (IDHS), and of external providers such as Aridhia's AnalytiXagility platform.
	## eMAP
	We are building EMAP as answer to the problem statement outlined above based on the following principles:
	1. Protection of operational systems 
	2. Protection of patient privacy:  
		A '*code to data*' rather than '*data to code*' paradigm
	3. Interoperability for semantic collaboration
	4. Scalable through open source
	
	![](DraggedImage.png)
	
	### 1. Protection of operational systems
	SQL (Structured Query Language) is the programming language found at the heart of most databases, healthcare related or otherwise. A SQL statement such as `SELECT * FROM PATIENTS` translates to English as 'give me everything stored in the patient data table' (the `*` is a wildcard that stands in for the names of all the specific data fields). For a hospital, this sort of query can be disastrous because while the database dutifully goes away to find all that information, no other user can make a request. A clinical user who reviews one patient at a time is unlikely to ask for so much data, but this is exactly the sort of query a researcher might require.[^4] 
	The widely implemented solution to this problem is to build a separate data store, or data warehouse. The operational systems are protected because they only need to be queried once to make an initial copy of the data. However, creating the data store is a Sisyphean task. In particular,  electronic data comes from disparate sources across the hospital, the data items need re-organising (transforming) before loaded into the store. This *Extract-Transform-Load* (ETL) process requires detailed knowledge of both the source data, and the destination schema. Such work is slow, expensive and requires updating each time there are changes at either end of the pipeline.
	We propose an alternative system based on a design implemented by a collaborative health science partnership in South Carolina.[^5] The key to this is attaching a 'carbon copier' module (CC module) to the hospital integration engine. The integration engine is the hospital's electronic Babel Fish. Electronic systems within the hospital are already in constant communication with each other. They exchange messages according to a loosely defined standard known as [HL7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_Level_7). Because the standardisation is poor, then an integration engine (SIP) is placed in the network to translate each message.[^6] The CC module simply makes a real time copy of each message flowing through the integration engine, and places that copy in a *shadow data store*.
	This has the following advantages:
	- data is made available to secondary users in near *real time*
	- the system is *scalable* in that data from most future systems will also flow through the integration engine
	- the system is *sustainable* in that the rich information in each message is preserved and can be parsed incrementally as additional resource becomes available
	- applications and analysis built on top of the CC module are *protected* in that they are isolated from modifications of the source systems
	- applications and analyses are *transportable* in that the CC module could be deployed (with minor adjustments) to other hospital's integration engines  
	This approach to capturing *data in transit* will replace, in many instances, the need to query *data at rest* using the ETL paradigm. Where data never leaves the source system, conventional ETL procedures will also add to the shadow data store thus ensuring that all necessary data are available to researchers and alike.
	### 2. Code to data[^7]
	We propose building two parallel shadow data stores (SDS): a *live* and a *mock* version. Both systems will exist within the hospital's digital infrastructure with all existing access controls and authentication procedures. The mock SDS will only ever contain simulated or de-identified data.
	Crucially, the mock SDS will be *air locked* from UCLH operational systems *and* accessible externally through a reverse proxy[^8]. Users will be able to install Linux based analysis and application frameworks, use version control and integrated testing, and collaborate with each other. 
	The architecture of the *mock* and the *live* stores would be managed by the hospital's digital service provider (Atos) and always in sync. As applications became ready for deployment, they would be packaged within dockerised containers. [Containerisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating-system-level_virtualization) is a recent software development that allows small packages of code to move from one environment to another along with all necessary dependencies. It is more flexible and less resource intense than the older approach of simulating the entire remote computer as a local virtual machine. 
	Just as the *live* and the *mock* data stores remain in sync, two *generic application environments* that receive these containerised code packages will also remain in sync. The air locked environment will contain the *mock* data and a mirrored *generic application environment*. Within this, analysts and developers will be able to develop and test their work collaboratively, deploy modern machine learning and data science libraries, and test and quality assure their work. Deployment across the airlock will be guaranteed to be problem free since the dependencies move with the code in containers, and the schema for the live and shadow data will be in lockstep. 
	Finally, the air locked environment will be documented using automated build scripts. These scripts will be accessible so that external collaborators from academia and industry will be able to replicate locally their own versions of the development environment. This will facilitate much wider collaboration, and much more rapid development cycles. 
	
	### 3. Interoperability
	Interoperability is the third defining principle of the platform. Bespoke code and non-standard data schemas are clear and obvious barriers to collaboration. We would neither be able to share analytical models nor user facing applications with collaborators. We would be unable to perform distributed analyses across health care networks (e.g. London Cancer, the NIHR Health Informatics Collaborative partners at other Biomedical Research Centres, or internationally).  We would be unable to recycle and reuse existing tools that have been developed elsewhere.
	The shadow data store will follow an open source schema that is being actively developed by the OHDSI programme  (Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics).[^9] This is already being used by UCL's CALIBER platform hosted at the Farr Institute of Health Informatics, the MIMIC critical care database at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), and an honour roll of other academic and industry partners.[^10]
	Moreover,  the Common Data Model (CDM) used by OHDSI is built on existing internationally standardised terminologies including SNOMED so that each data item acquires semantic meaning. SNOMED is the agreed terminology of NHS digital, and NHS secondary care organisations will be required to adopt this by April 2020.[^11]
	
	### 4. Scalable
	#### Scaling out
	The fourth and final principle is that the design is scalable through open source. We imagine future collaborations between hospitals across local networks. Each will have their own systems, and some their electronic health care record providers. However, each will have its own integration engine also dealing in HL7 messages. Patient demographics, inpatient transfers, outpatient bookings, pathology results, radiology reports and more will flow through that engine.
	Because just the CC module interfaces with the local systems, then all other data processing tools, terminology mapping procedures,  and derived products including analytical models, and reporting method will continue to work. Because the data is standardised then network wide queries can be performed, and patient level analyses across sites would be possible. Because the platform is built using open source software then there is no commercial lock in, and modifications and updates can be shared.
	#### Scaling up
	This is admittedly a grand vision of scaling, but the system is scalable and sustainable at the other extreme too. The initial offering does not need to harvest, standardise, and process every data item. A minimum viable product (MVP) will construct a master patient index (MPI) from the message stream, and store the carbon copied message in a data lake.  The MPI would be propagated to the live shadow data store, and the structure (not the content) of this index replicated in the mock version. Containerised packages of code would move across the airlock between the mirrored generic application environment. Incrementally, research teams would develop the code to parse the unread content of messages in the data lake, map this to standard terminologies, and load the observations into the SDS. This code would continue to run for the next team who would extend the work as they needed. Each team would benefit from the work of others.
	
	## eMAP project status
	eMAP has been  funded by UCLH charity as the infrastructure component of a project called *Inform*.  We have worked with UCLH digital services, the Clinical Research Informatics Unit, and Atos (as the digital service provider) on the design of the platform  since December 2017. 
	The *Inform* team have a clinical base in critical care, and have been running the Critical Care theme of the NIHR Health Informatics Collaborative since 2014. Because critical care already have an electronic health record, then eMAP is  using these data as a test case. A Health Foundation funded project to forecast critical care occupancy and improve patient flow will provide the applied test of the message streams to the containerised analytical modules. However, this is in no way a programme specific to a single clinical domain. We are building the foundation of a programme that should be equally relevant for all specialties and teams across the organisation. 
	The programme of work is in five parts and we have an ambitious timeline that sees a minimum viable product by Autumn 2018. Parts 1-3 are already in progress.
	1. the infrastructure to host eMAP
	2. the containerisation architecture 
	3. the HL7 message feed from the integration engine (CC module)
	4. the internal facing and interoperable SDS
	5. the external facing mock SDS[^12]

# Learning statistics in a pandemic

So there’s a global pandemic. Your first task is to report the mortality rate. The government will only be convinced to act if the mortality is greater than that for seasonal flu (approximately 1%).

You have a colleague in Wuhan. She struggles to send you data because she’s worried about censorship so you communicate with a simple code using Twitter. If the last character of the tweet is a punctuation mark or emoji that means a case of COVID-19 admitted to her hospital has died. If the last character is not a punctuation mark or emoji, then the patient has been discharged alive.
 
Here are the  first 3 tweets from her.

> Hi. How are you?

> It’s cold. Say hi to your family!

> Better day today, warmer

So we read this as 

* Died
* Died
* Survived

From now on, we’re going to represent this as a string of characters `DDS`. You receive 7 more tweets over the next couple of days: `DDSDSSDDDS` . That is 6 deaths and 4 survivors, or a 60% mortality rate.

Let’s recap.
1. We have some measurements or observations (our *data*).
2. We want to know the ‘true’ mortality rate, and are nervous about causing unnecessary alarm.

Point (2) is crucial because in framing the question, we are acknowledging that we have uncertainty. From our perspective, the true mortality rate should not be reported as a single number (in this case 6/10 or 60%). That might be true, but it excludes our uncertainty. It would be an incomplete description rather like saying the latitude and longitude of London is (0º,0º). That is not even the latitude and longitude of the Greenwich Observatory because both the Observatory and London are not single points in space. They have a spread from north to south and east to west.

To capture uncertainty, we must treat the true mortality rate as a range, or distribution, of values. Not all values in the range are equally plausible even before we observe any data. The mortality cannot be less than 0% or greater than 100% so our **prior** belief (p) lies in the range 0 ≤ *p* ≤ 1.  

Let’s recap again. We now have two useful tools.
1. Data
2. A prior (belief) about the mortality rate.

We will use the data to update our prior, and you will not be surprised to learn that we will call the result the **posterior** (probability distribution). The more data we have, the more we can pin down our prior. Let’s take the outcomes for the first three patients as an example.

1. Our initial prior says the risk of death is anywhere from 0 ≤ *p* ≤ 1.
2. The first and second patients both died. It’s not a lot of information but we can at least say the risk of death cannot be zero. We now believe *p* lies in the range 0 < *p* ≤ 1.
3. The third patient survived so similarly we *p* must now lie in the range 0 < *p* < 1.

This discrete logic, ruling in and ruling out certain values based on observations gets us so far. But there is more information still in just these first  three cases `DDS`. We need a tool that connects the count of deaths to our *prior.* The more data we see, the more important this will become. Three cases becomes ten cases with six deaths  (`DDSDSSDDDS`). But the tweets don’t stop there. When our final sample becomes 1000 cases with 600 deaths, the proportion does not change. But we will be much, much more worried because we have an intuition that the proportion from the bigger sample is a more certain estimate. 

So how do we connect the observed data to our beliefs. We need to describe a mechanic m for generating the data. The mechanism must only be based on things that we can verify, or are happy to assume. So one mechanism might be that a divine being ordered there six deaths in this specific sequence. Could be true but it doesn't really help move us forwards.. A better mechanism is to imagine a series of coin flips with a special coin that is weighted to show tails in the same proportion that deaths occur.
(see "county deaths")
This model creates a connection between the data and the mortality rate, and it does so with the minimum of prior assumptions (see maximum information entropy). for example, imagine that we knew the mortality rate was 50 % . The model tells us how that data would have to come about.

We see that many more paths arrive at 6 than 1 or 2 or 3 death, for example. But we
also note that 5 deaths is the commonest finding. Our intuition tells us that our data (our observation) provide quite good evidence for-a mortality rate of 50%. but very weak evidence for mortality rates of 10,20 or so, 90" I..
